Enjoy this final stretch and keep up the fantastic work!I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's really cool to be a part of it. Looking back, I didn't think I'd be interested in research when I was a freshman. I enjoyed coding projects and hackathons, but I didn't see research as something that aligned with my interests. However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience. She mentioned there was an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant because research seemed intimidating, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists collaborate with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We work together to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In contrast to the small datasets we often work with in classes, our datasets are tens of terabytes in size. Visualizing such large datasets so that domain experts can quickly extract insights is a significant challenge. One of my main tasks involves developing front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. This requires expertise in advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.The first research project I really got into involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had a vast amount of daily temperature readings from buoys scattered across the Pacific. The raw data was enormous, consisting of numerous files spread across different servers, each representing a single day's worth of readings at minute intervals. Our task was to aggregate and present the data in a coherent manner, allowing researchers to identify patterns over months or even years. I dove headfirst into the project, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and designing interfaces that enabled researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. It was a surreal experience seeing my name in an official publication, and it remains one of my proudest moments in college.My current research has shifted to immersive analytics platforms, which explore how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' understanding of complex data. It's fascinating to think about how looking at raw numerical data in a spreadsheet is one thing, and 2D visuals like graphs are another step up. However, being able to walk around and interact with a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment could be a game-changer for certain fields. This is a significant leap from just coding websites. My work involves a lot of experimentation, such as plugging in VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's all cutting-edge, which makes it exciting. Since there isn't a well-established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet, every day feels like forging my own path.Research life is often misunderstood as me sitting in a quiet corner coding away on some mysterious project. However, it's actually a lot of reading. Academic papers never seem to end, and when I'm trying to solve a bug with rendering volumetric data in VR, there's a good chance someone has attempted something similar and written about it in a conference proceeding or workshop. I need to comb through these papers to find relevant information. It can be overwhelming, but over time, you learn how to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine if a paper is relevant before diving into the details. Occasionally, when I find something interesting, I'll share it with the rest of the lab, and we'll discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.I've also had the opportunity to present at a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus. It was a great experience, as it forced me to distill complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was nervous, but it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People were genuinely interested in what I was doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who attended, and they shared some interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to the potential for research to transition from academia to real-world applications.
